messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: We got our first GDPR erasure request, and it turns out Remove on the user
list doesn't remove anyone — it flips `active` off and scrambles the email,
and everything else stays.

Make it actually erase: nothing of theirs is left anywhere — not a row, not
a stale search hit. One exception: books they created that are shared with
everyone keep working — people are reading those. Take their name off and
byline them "Deleted author".

One wrinkle: most of the requests we owe are people someone already "removed"
the old way — deactivated, email rewritten to `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@...`.
It has to work for them too, and their sign-in log entries sit under the
address they actually signed in with.

Use `assert_in_body` and `assert_not_in_body` to check if text is present or absent in the response body without DOM manipulation.

```ruby
assert_in_body "Expected content"
assert_not_in_body "Unexpected content"
```

```ruby
assert_includes response.body, "Expected content"
```

### Simplified respond_to Blocks
When using `respond_to` with default rendering, omit the `{ render }` block as it's implied.

**Preferred:**
```ruby
def show
  respond_to do |format|
    format.html
    format.md
  end
end
```

**Avoid:**
```ruby
def show
  respond_to do |format|
    format.html { render }
    format.md { render }

end
```

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

require "test_helper"

class UsersControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup do
    @join_code = accounts(:signal).join_code
  end

  test "new" do
    get join_url(@join_code)
    assert_response :success
  end

  test "new does not allow a signed in user" do
    sign_in :david

    get join_url(@join_code)
    assert_redirected_to root_url
  end

  test "new requires a join code" do
    get join_url("not")
    assert_response :not_found
  end

  test "create" do
    assert_difference -> { User.count }, 1 do
      post join_url(@join_code), params: { user: { name: "New Person", email_address: "new@example.com", password: "secret123456" } }
    end

    assert_redirected_to root_url

    user = User.last
    assert_equal user.id, Session.find_by(token: parsed_cookies.signed[:session_token]).user.id
  end

  test "creating a new user with an existing email address redirects to login screen" do
    assert_no_difference -> { User.count } do
      post join_url(@join_code), params: { user: { name: "Another David", email_address: users(:david).email_address, password: "secret123456" } }
    end

    assert_redirected_to new_session_url(email_address: users(:david).email_address)
  end

  test "update" do
    sign_in :david
    assert users(:david).administrator?

    put user_url(users(:kevin)), params: { user: { role: "administrator" } }

    assert_redirected_to users_url
    assert users(:kevin).reload.administrator?
  end

  test "update does not allow non-admins to change roles" do
    sign_in :kevin
    assert_not users(:kevin).administrator?

    put user_url(users(:kevin)), params: { user: { role: "administrator" } }

    assert_response :forbidden
    assert_not users(:kevin).reload.administrator?
  end

  test "destroy" do
    sign_in :david

    assert_difference -> { User.active.count }, -1 do
      delete user_url(users(:kevin))
    end

    assert_redirected_to users_url
    assert_nil User.active.find_by(id: users(:kevin).id)
  end

  test "destroy is not allowed to non-admins" do
    sign_in :kevin

    delete user_url(users(:david))
    assert_response :forbidden
  end
end

  before_action :broadcast_being_edited_indicator, only: :update
  after_action :remember_reading_position, only: :show, if: :signed_in?

      format.html
      format.md

  end

    respond_to do |format|
      format.turbo_stream { render }
      format.html { head :no_content }
    end
  end

  def destroy
    @leaf.trashed!

    respond_to do |format|
      format.turbo_stream { render }
      format.html { redirect_to book_slug_url(@book) }
    end
  end

  private
    def leaf_params
      default_leaf_params.merge params.fetch(:leaf, {}).permit(:title)

      if position = params[:position]&.to_i

      end
    end

    def remember_reading_position
      ReadingMark.remember @leaf
    end

    def broadcast_being_edited_indicator
      Turbo::StreamsChannel.broadcast_render_later_to @leaf, :being_edited,

**Database and Codebase Deep Dive**

Okay, let's break this down systematically. My immediate thought is to create a complete mental map of the entire data structure and codebase. This means going beyond the superficial and diving deep into all the foreign keys, associations, virtual tables, ActiveStorage interactions (blobs, attachments, and their variants), and potential caching mechanisms across the entire system. I need to understand *every* table and its relationship to others, especially how destroy operations cascade.

First, I'll start with the `db/schema.rb` file. Here's what I see:

*   **Users:** `users` table with standard fields like name, email, password, role, active status, and timestamps.
*   **Sessions:**  `sessions` table related to `users` via a foreign key (`user_id`). Important fields include token, IP address, user agent, and activity timestamps.
*   **Sign-In Events:** This table, `sign_in_events`, is interesting because it *doesn't* have a direct foreign key to `users`. It relies on matching the email address. That could be a source of inconsistency.
*   **Accesses:** The `accesses` table connects users to books via foreign keys (`user_id` and `book_id`). Level of access and timestamps.
*   **Reading Marks:** A key table (`reading_marks`) that relates users to leaves via a foreign key (`user_id` and `leaf_id` with `on_delete: :cascade`). We'll have to investigate how a cascaded delete on a `leaf` affects the `reading_marks`.
*   **Books:** The `books` table is central. Besides the core attributes like title, author, and publication date, it includes a `creator_id` foreign key referencing `users`. Critically, it uses `has_one_attached :cover` for ActiveStorage attachments, plus `has_many :leaves` with `dependent: :destroy` and `has_many :accesses` with `dependent: :destroy`.
*   **Leaves:** A polymorphic table (`leafable_type`, `leafable_id`) that belongs to books via `book_id` foreign key. Important to note is `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all`! That's a potential area for data integrity issues if not handled carefully. Also there is an `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?` callback. That will also require careful examination. I should check if `Leaf` has `has_many :reading_marks`.
*   **Edits:** The `edits` table has `leaf_id` linking to `leaves` and a polymorphic association to `leafable`. I need to figure out exactly how the `dependent: :destroy` setting on `Edit` interacts with `leafable`. Since we know that we have `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` in the `leaf`, will the `leafable` record be removed? Also, how are deletes from `Leaf` or `Book` handled?
*   **Pages:** The pages table, using `has_markdown :body` to ActionText/Markdown.  It has `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy` for more ActiveStorage integration.
*   **Pictures:** `pictures` uses `has_one_attached :image`.
*   **Sections:** Very simple table to store section data.
*   **ActionText Markdown:** `action_text_markdowns` stores the Markdown content.
*   **Active Storage:**  We have the standard ActiveStorage tables: `active_storage_attachments`, `active_storage_blobs`, and `active_storage_variant_records`. I need to verify that `dependent: :purge_later` is the default in Rails for attachments, specifically, that `has_one_attached :cover, dependent: :purge_later` on `Book` actually works, and whether `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy` on `ActionText::Markdown` also uses a default setting. And same with the `image`.
*   **Leaf Search Index:** The `leaf_search_index` is a virtual table (FTS5). The title and content are important. Also, what happens when `Book` or `Leaf` are destroyed with regards to this index? And is this index updated when the data changes?

Now, I need to zoom in on how these destroy operations actually play out in real life. I need to know *exactly* what happens when a `Book` is destroyed, and how that affects its associated `Leaves`, `Edits`, `ReadingMarks`, ActiveStorage objects, and this `leaf_search_index`.

Okay, let's break this down meticulously. My primary objective is to implement a robust GDPR erasure process. I need to make sure *nothing* is left behind, except for the specified exception. I'll need to handle both active and already-deactivated users, and to thoroughly analyze every possible way a user might be erased.

First, I need to understand what's happening right now with the current `UsersController#destroy` and `User#destroy` methods. Currently, `UsersController#destroy` *deactivates* the user. It looks like it will need a complete overhaul to fulfill the GDPR requirements.

I have to carefully consider all of the database associations on the `User` model. Right now, `User#destroy` uses `dependent: :destroy` for sessions and accesses, and this is good. I need to make sure that order of operations is respected so that sign-in events don't have residual references to the `user` table. However, it looks like `reading_marks` currently lacks a `dependent` clause and will raise an error. That needs to be addressed.

Critically, there's `created_books`.  The prompt specifies that books shared with everyone should remain, but the creator's identity should be removed and the author should be replaced with "Deleted author." Let's re-read to be extra sure: it's not simply removing the creator; it's also updating the `author` field. I need to handle those books carefully. I'll need to update them, setting `creator_id` to `nil` and the `author` to `"Deleted author"`, while leaving `everyone_access: true` books intact. I'll have to make sure that the cache invalidates on these books to reflect the changes. I'll need to be aware of how the search indexes react to changes. I need to confirm that `created_books` will destroy *non-everyone* books! This also means verifying the implications of `published` status for any books that *are* kept, and how access rights are updated.

**GDPR Erasure Deep Dive**

Okay, so we've got a GDPR erasure request and it's time to make sure we're actually *erasing* data, not just hiding it. Let's make sure we're covering ALL bases here and leave NOTHING behind. First, let's break down the requirements, point by point, making sure we haven't overlooked any edge cases or implications:

1.  We *need* to be erasing data, not just deactivating or scrambling things. Flipping an `active` flag isn't cutting it.
2.  Nothing. Absolutely *nothing* of the user's should remain. No rows, no stale search hits, the whole nine yards.
3.  The exception? Shared books. Those have to keep working, but we need to anonymize them, replacing the author name with "Deleted author."
4.  And *crucially*, we have to handle the existing "removals" – the deactivated users with scrambled emails. We need to make sure this process works retroactively and that it also works with sign-in logs tied to their original email.

Now, let's dive into the specifics of this "nothing left" requirement. Starting with the *`not a row, not a stale search hit`* part.

I need to focus on how we're currently handling data destruction when a `User` is wiped. Let's start with `Book` and `Leaf` relationships. Specifically, I'm thinking about the cascading deletes and search indexing. For example, if a `Book` is destroyed, its associated `Leaves` are also destroyed due to `dependent: :destroy`.

But then, I notice `Leaf` has `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?`. This is an issue.

Hold on. `Leaf#searchable?` is simply based on the `searchable_content`. Delegated types add another wrinkle, and Rails has a specific destruction order, so I need to check the order of destruction.

My immediate concern is the order of events when destroying a `Leaf`. Does the `dependent: :destroy` on `leafable` happen *before* or *after* `after_destroy_commit`? What is the impact of a transaction? Let's trace `leaf.destroy` and make sure it is happening in the correct order.

Here's the problem: The `leaf.destroy` starts a transaction. Then, the `dependent: :destroy` (on `leaf.leafable`) is called, meaning the dependent `Page` or `Section` is destroyed as well. Wait! `Page` and `Section` likely have their own cascade, so that destruction takes place as well, and there is a `markdown_body` field which is destroyed too! This may be an issue.

So, in that exact order, what is `leaf.searchable_content` returning *after* the `Leaf`, the `leafable` (`Page` or `Section`), and the `markdown_body` have already been destroyed? Is that even possible? Does Rails handle the `dependent: :destroy` with a clean up or something?

I need to immediately test this in the `bin/rails runner` environment.

I also have other concerns. What if `Leaf` destruction happens *inside* a transaction? Or what if there's still a row lingering in `leaf_search_index` because `searchable_content` ends up as `nil` or `""` or `after_destroy_commit` simply didn't run? Or worse, what if that `after_destroy_commit` evaluated the `if: :searchable?` condition *after* the destruction of the data? Or what if, for some reason, the index still *had* data even if the content became empty?

I need to test this right now in `bin/rails runner` to see what is happening!

  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  REBALANCE_THRESHOLD = 1e-10
  ELEMENT_GAP         = 1

  included do
    scope :positioned, -> { order(:position_score, :id) }

    scope :before, ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score < ?", other.position_score) }
    scope :after,  ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score > ?", other.position_score) }

    around_create :insert_at_default_position
    after_save_commit :rebalance_positions, if: :rebalance_required?
  end

  class_methods do
    def positioned_within(parent, association:, filter:)
      define_method :positioning_parent do
        send(parent)
      end

      define_method :all_positioned_siblings do
        positioning_parent.send(association).send(filter).positioned
      end

      define_method :other_positioned_siblings do
        all_positioned_siblings.excluding(self)
      end

      private :positioning_parent, :all_positioned_siblings, :other_positioned_siblings
    end
  end

  def previous
    other_positioned_siblings.before(self).last
  end

  def next
    other_positioned_siblings.after(self).first
  end

  def move_to_position(offset, followed_by: [])
    with_positioning_lock do
      all_to_move = [ self, *followed_by ]
      before, after = before_and_after_for(offset: offset, moving: all_to_move)
      gap = (after - before) / (all_to_move.count + 1)

      all_to_move.each.with_index(1) do |item, index|
        item.update!(position_score: before + (index * gap))
      end

      remember_to_rebalance_positions if gap < REBALANCE_THRESHOLD
    end
  end

  def position_as_percentage
    100 * ordinal_position.to_f / all_positioned_siblings.count
  end

  private
    def ordinal_position
      other_positioned_siblings.before(self).count + 1
    end

    def insert_at_default_position
      with_positioning_lock do
        position_at_end
        yield
      end
    end

    def position_at_start
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)) - ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def position_at_end
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score) || 0) + ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def before_and_after_for(offset:, moving:)
      other_items = all_positioned_siblings.excluding(moving)

      if offset < 1
        after = all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)
        before = after - ELEMENT_GAP
      else
        before, after = other_items.offset(offset - 1).limit(2).pluck(:position_score)
        before ||= all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score)
        after ||= before + (moving.count.succ * ELEMENT_GAP)
      end

      [ before, after ]
    end

    def remember_to_rebalance_positions
      @rebalance_required = true
    end

    def rebalance_required?
      @rebalance_required
    end

    def rebalance_positions
      with_positioning_lock do
        odered = all_positioned_siblings.select("row_number() over (order by position_score, id) as new_score, id")
        sql = "update #{self.class.table_name} set position_score = new_score from (#{odered.to_sql}) as ordered where #{self.class.table_name}.id = ordered.id"

        self.class.connection.execute sql
      end
      @rebalance_required = false
    end

    def with_positioning_lock(&block)
      positioning_parent.with_lock &block
    end

Alright, let's get down to brass tacks. We've got a GDPR erasure request, and we need to make sure we're scrubbing *everything* related to a user. This isn't just a matter of flipping a flag and rewriting an email; we're talking full data annihilation.

*   **Books:** If a user created a book, depending on its "everyone\_access" status, the outcome varies. If public, the book stays, but the author is "Deleted author." if Private, the book is deleted, along with all of its dependent data.
*   **Accesses:** The user's access records are gone. If the deleted user only has read/edit access, their access row on other's books are also deleted.
*   **Reading Marks:** All the user's reading marks across any book are also deleted.

Next, I need to make sure I get the edge cases. I can see a LOT of opportunity for subtle data leakage and corner cases, and I can't let anything slip through the cracks:

*   **Orphaned Books:** What happens if a user is gone, but *other* users still have access to one of their "private" books (that somehow got kept around)? The book itself, and all access rights must also be removed.
*   **"Deactivated" Users:** We've got the whole "deactivated" email thing with a UUID. I've got to make sure the deletion logic works for those legacy deactivated users as well as for active ones. I have to think very carefully about the order of deletion to prevent weird situations where we try to delete something that no longer exists (and also be certain that *every* related record is destroyed).

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process on tackling this user erasure issue. First, I realized a crucial detail regarding `ActiveStorage` and variants. When a blob is purged, which happens when a variant record is destroyed, the associated `PurgeJob` is enqueued asynchronously. To ensure synchronous purging, especially during user deletion, I need to collect and purge variant blobs *before* the main blobs. That way, all associated `ActiveStorage` data is cleaned up immediately, guaranteeing no lingering orphaned records. This approach avoids potential race conditions and ensures data consistency throughout the process.

Now, let's consider edge cases. I needed to meticulously examine scenarios where the application state might affect user deletion. Specifically, what happens if the last user, an admin, or the currently signed-in user is being deleted? The `sessions_controller_test.rb` provided a valuable clue: `User.destroy_all`. This showed that destroying all users redirects to the first run URL, indicating a clean state. This scenario confirmed that a robust cleanup can handle complete user removal.

Next, I delved into the `users_controller_test.rb`. It highlighted a critical consideration: a comprehensive test suite. My goal here is to expand the existing test to cover all aspects of user deletion, including row deletion, session removal, access removal, reading mark removal, and, critically, `SignInEvent` deletion. I have to ensure private books created by the user are *completely* gone, including associated files, variants, and search indexes. Conversely, I must confirm that shared books are properly anonymized with "Deleted author" and `creator: nil` and remain accessible to other users.

Furthermore, I have to ensure that users who have already been "deactivated" can also be completely erased. module User::Authoring
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  DELETED_AUTHOR_NAME = "Deleted author"

  included do
    has_many :created_books, class_name: "Book", foreign_key: :creator_id,
      inverse_of: :creator

    has_many :reading_marks, dependent: :delete_all

    before_destroy :anonymize_or_destroy_created_books
  end

  private
    def anonymize_or_destroy_created_books
      created_books.with_everyone_access.find_each do |book|
        book.update!(creator: nil, author: DELETED_AUTHOR_NAME)
      end

      private_books = created_books.where(everyone_access: false).to_a
      blob_ids = private_books.flat_map { |book| blob_ids_for_book(book) }.uniq
      variant_blob_ids = variant_blob_ids_for(blob_ids)

      private_books.each(&:destroy!)

      purge_unattached_blobs(blob_ids)
      purge_unattached_blobs(variant_blob_ids)
    end

    def blob_ids_for_book(book)
      leaf_ids = book.leaves.pluck(:id)
      picture_ids = book.leaves.where(leafable_type: "Picture").pluck(:leafable_id) +
                    Edit.where(leaf_id: leaf_ids, leafable_type: "Picture").pluck(:leafable_id)
      page_ids = book.leaves.where(leafable_type: "Page").pluck(:leafable_id) +
                 Edit.where(leaf_id: leaf_ids, leafable_type: "Page").pluck(:leafable_id)
      markdown_ids = ActionText::Markdown.where(record_type: "Page", record_id: page_ids.uniq).pluck(:id)

      ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Book", record_id: book.id)
        .or(ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Picture", record_id: picture_ids.uniq))
        .or(ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "ActionText::Markdown", record_id: markdown_ids))
        .distinct
        .pluck(:blob_id)
    end

    def variant_blob_ids_for(blob_ids)
      return [] if blob_ids.empty?

      ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(
        record_type: "ActiveStorage::VariantRecord",
        record_id: ActiveStorage::VariantRecord.where(blob_id: blob_ids).select(:id)
      ).pluck(:blob_id)
    end

    def purge_unattached_blobs(blob_ids)
      return if blob_ids.empty?

      ActiveStorage::Blob.where(id: blob_ids).find_each do |blob|
        blob.purge if blob.attachments.none?
      end
    end
end

      end
    end

      execute_sql_with_binds "insert into leaf_search_index(rowid, title, content ) values (?, ?, ?)",
        id, sanitize_for_index(title), sanitize_for_index(searchable_content)
    end

    def update_in_search_index
      transaction do
        updated = execute_sql_with_binds "update leaf_search_index set title = ?, content = ? where rowid = ?",
          sanitize_for_index(title), sanitize_for_index(searchable_content), id

      terms.sort_by(&:length).reverse
    end

    class_methods do

        def remove_invalid_search_characters(terms)

        def remove_unbalanced_quotes(terms)

messages.thinking:
**The Rails `belongs_to :creator` Mystery!**

Okay, so I just stumbled upon something pretty significant in our Rails app. It's about how we handle the `creator` association with our `Book` model, specifically the `belongs_to` declaration. I'm seeing that using `default: -> { Current.user }` within `belongs_to` is causing a subtle but serious bug, especially when it comes to anonymizing users and their created content.

Here's the problem: that `default:` is sneaky. It doesn't *just* run on create; it's firing during `before_validation` *even on update* if the `creator` is `nil`. So, when we're trying to anonymize a user, and we do something like `book.update!(creator: nil, ...)`, the `default:` kicks in and *silently* reassigns the `creator` back to the current user (which is the admin deleting the account!). We would have been in a world of hurt if that integration test wasn't there to catch this.

The current setup in `Book::Authorship` is the culprit. We have `belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", inverse_of: :created_books, optional: true, default: -> { Current.user }`. This *seemed* like the right approach, defaulting the `creator` on new book creations. But it's biting us during updates, too.

The fix I'm seeing is surprisingly clean: We need to change *how* we default the creator. If we tweak `Book::Authorship` to use `before_validation(on: :create) { self.creator ||= Current.user }` instead, we get the desired behavior:

*   Creating a book will default `creator` to `Current.user` if not explicitly set to `nil` or another user.
*   Updating a book (including our anonymization updates where we set `creator: nil`) will *not* reassign the creator. This allows us to correctly set the creator to `nil` when anonymizing.
*   In `User::Authoring`, we'll be able to successfully update `creator_id` to `nil`.

I've confirmed that using `before_validation(on: :create)` fixes the issue because the `default:` option in `belongs_to` adds a `before_validation` callback, which we want to restrict to runs only during creation. Now, updates won't overwrite `creator_id` to `Current.user` when it's `nil`.

I'm confident that this resolves the bug. Let's update that file and rerun all our tests, including rubocop and brakeman, just to be absolutely sure.

    before_validation(on: :create) { self.creator ||= Current.user }
  end
end
